title: Joseph: Dreams and Betrayal
rules: Existing native Story wheel, sizing, rewards and three contextual hints (free / 15 / 25 Insight Tokens). Native full reveal costs 25 Points. Development entry only; unlock after Episode 13. No unrelated modes or public loader changes.
completionMessage: You've followed Joseph from the flocks of Canaan to a household in Egypt. His brothers' betrayal has changed his life, but the dreams haven't been fulfilled. Next, we'll follow his life in Potiphar's house. That episode is still being prepared.

discoveries.title: A Young Shepherd Speaks Up
discoveries.narration: Joseph is 17, and we're joining him among his father's flocks in Canaan. He's working with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah. Something about their conduct isn't right, and he brings troubling news back to his father.

interaction.prompt: What did Joseph bring his father about the conduct of the brothers he worked with?

progressiveHints.text: Think of information brought back to someone who wasn't there.
It described the brothers' conduct, not the size of the flock.
This word can mean an account of what someone has seen or learned.

discoveries.explanation: Joseph brought a bad report about those brothers to his father. Genesis doesn't tell us exactly what they'd done, so we shouldn't fill in the details. We meet Joseph as a young shepherd willing to bring unwelcome news home, not as Egypt's future ruler.

discoveries.title: A Family Pulling Apart
discoveries.narration: Jacob has a special robe made for Joseph. His brothers can see that their father loves Joseph more than his other sons, and they can't speak peaceably to him. A gift that sets one son apart has become part of a painful family division.

interaction.prompt: Which strong feeling toward Joseph went beyond disagreement and kept his brothers from speaking peaceably to him?

progressiveHints.text: Their reaction was directed at Joseph himself, not just at the garment.
It's stronger than annoyance and the opposite of brotherly love.
Genesis says they began to hate him. Build the noun for that feeling.

discoveries.explanation: Their feeling was hatred. Jacob loved Joseph especially because he was a son of his old age, and the special robe made that favor visible. The brothers' refusal to speak peaceably shows how deep the division had become. It doesn't excuse the choices they'll make next.

discoveries.title: Bundles in a Dream
discoveries.narration: Now Joseph tells his brothers about an unusual dream. They're out in a field, gathering cut grain into bundles. His bundle stands upright, while theirs gather around and bow down. Can you see why his brothers connect this picture with someone ruling over them?

interaction.prompt: What are the tied bundles of harvested grain in Joseph's first dream called?

progressiveHints.text: These are gathered stalks from a harvest, not living trees.
The word names bundles of cut grain tied together.
Use the plural: one bundle stands upright while the others bow around it.

discoveries.explanation: Sheaves are bundles of harvested grain. In Joseph's dream, his brothers' sheaves bowed to his, and they understood the picture as him ruling over them. They weren't watching this happen in a real field—it was a dream Joseph related to them. Their response was still more hatred.

discoveries.title: A Second Picture in the Sky
discoveries.narration: The next dream takes us from a field to the sky: the sun, the moon, and 11 smaller lights bow down to Joseph. Jacob rebukes him when he hears it. Yet there's another detail worth noticing—his father keeps the saying in mind.

interaction.prompt: Which heavenly objects numbered 11 in Joseph's second dream?

progressiveHints.text: Leave out the two larger lights; the question asks about the group of 11.
These lights often appear together in the night sky.
The dream names the sun, the moon, and 11 of these.

discoveries.explanation: There were 11 stars, along with the sun and moon. Jacob connected the dream with members of the family bowing to Joseph. He rebuked Joseph but also kept the saying in mind. Notice the difference: the brothers grew jealous, while Jacob didn't simply dismiss what he'd heard.

discoveries.title: The Search Goes Farther
discoveries.narration: Jacob sends Joseph from the valley of Hebron to check on his brothers and the flock near Shechem. But they aren't there. A man finds Joseph looking for them in a field and tells him where they've gone. Joseph follows that lead instead of turning for home.

interaction.prompt: Where did Joseph finally find his brothers after looking near Shechem?

progressiveHints.text: This is the second place in his search, not where his father first sent him.
A man in a field had heard the brothers name this destination.
Joseph went after them there; it wasn't Hebron, where his journey began.

discoveries.explanation: Joseph found them at Dothan. He'd first gone toward Shechem, then continued after a man told him where they'd moved. Jacob's request was to learn whether his sons and the flock were well. Joseph followed through on that errand even when the first stop didn't bring him to them.

discoveries.title: A Plan to Bring Him Home
discoveries.narration: Before Joseph reaches them, his brothers are already plotting to kill him. One brother speaks against taking his life. He suggests putting Joseph into a waterpit without harming him. Genesis lets us know what he's really trying to do: get Joseph safely back to their father.

interaction.prompt: Which brother proposed the waterpit because he intended to rescue Joseph and return him to Jacob?

progressiveHints.text: This brother opposed the plan to take Joseph's life.
His plan was to bring Joseph back to their father, not sell him to traders.
Later, this same brother returned to the pit and was distressed to find Joseph gone.

discoveries.explanation: Reuben was trying to rescue Joseph. His suggestion about the pit wasn't the whole plan—Genesis explicitly says he intended to return Joseph to their father. Judah's later proposal was different: sell Joseph. Keeping those two proposals separate helps us follow what each brother actually did.

discoveries.title: An Empty Pit
discoveries.narration: When Joseph arrives, the brothers strip off his special robe and throw him into a pit. There's a small but important detail in the account: it's empty, with no water in it. Joseph is still alive, but his brothers have put him where he can't simply continue his errand.

interaction.prompt: What kind of storage place, empty and dry at the time, did the brothers throw Joseph into?

progressiveHints.text: This was a place meant to hold a liquid, not an animal pen.
It was dug down into the ground, and there was no water inside.
Combine what it normally held with the word for a deep hole. The NWT uses this compound word.

discoveries.explanation: It was a waterpit—a place for holding water—but this one was dry. That detail matters: the brothers had put Joseph into confinement, not into water. They'd also taken his special robe. Reuben's rescue plan hadn't yet succeeded, and Joseph was still in danger.

discoveries.title: Traders on the Road
discoveries.narration: The brothers sit down to eat. Then they spot traders coming from Gilead, with camels carrying aromatic goods toward Egypt. Judah sees a way to get rid of Joseph without killing him: sell him. Calling Joseph their own flesh doesn't make that proposal kind.

interaction.prompt: What word describes the traveling group of merchants and loaded camels the brothers saw?

progressiveHints.text: Think of people and pack animals making a trading journey together.
This group came from Gilead and was traveling toward Egypt.
It's a traveling company of traders, not the name of a single merchant or his cargo.

discoveries.explanation: A caravan is a group traveling together, often with goods to trade. This one carried labdanum gum, balsam, and resinous bark toward Egypt. Its arrival gave Judah the opportunity to propose selling Joseph. Sparing someone's life doesn't make selling that person into slavery an act of kindness.

discoveries.title: A Brother Sold
discoveries.narration: Joseph is lifted out of the pit, but this isn't the rescue Reuben planned. He's sold for 20 pieces of a precious metal and taken toward Egypt. When Reuben later returns to the pit, Joseph is gone. Reuben tears his garments in distress.

interaction.prompt: Which metal was used for the 20 pieces paid when Joseph was sold?

progressiveHints.text: The price wasn't paid in livestock or grain.
It's a precious metal, but the passage doesn't say gold.
The NWT calls the payment 20 pieces of this metal; it doesn't describe minted coins.

discoveries.explanation: Joseph was sold for 20 pieces of silver. Genesis mentions both Midianite merchants and Ishmaelites in the trading account; it doesn't describe two separate sales at the pit. Reuben returned afterward and found Joseph gone. His distress reminds us that his intention to rescue Joseph hadn't protected him from the sale.

discoveries.title: Evidence That Misleads
discoveries.narration: The brothers now send an object home for Jacob to identify. They've deliberately changed it so he'll reach a terrible conclusion. What they send is real, but the impression they create is false. Jacob believes a wild animal has killed Joseph.

interaction.prompt: Which personal item did the brothers use to make Jacob believe Joseph had been killed?

progressiveHints.text: Jacob had originally had this item made especially for Joseph.
It was taken from Joseph before he was thrown into the pit.
It's the special outer garment, not a shepherd's staff or a pair of sandals.

discoveries.explanation: They used Joseph's robe, dipped in a male goat's blood. They asked Jacob to identify it, and he concluded that a wild animal had killed his son. The robe was genuine; the story it seemed to tell was false. Their deception hurt someone who hadn't seen what had actually happened.

discoveries.title: A Father's Sorrow
discoveries.narration: Jacob mourns for many days. His sons and daughters keep trying to comfort him, but he refuses to take comfort. We know Joseph is alive; Jacob doesn't. The brothers' deception has left their father suffering a loss that hasn't actually happened.

interaction.prompt: What word describes Jacob's deep sorrow as he mourned the son he believed was dead?

progressiveHints.text: This is an emotional response to losing someone, not a name for anger at an enemy.
It explains why words of comfort didn't simply end his mourning.
Think of the deep sorrow people experience when someone they love has died.

discoveries.explanation: Jacob's grief was real, even though Joseph hadn't died. He tore his garments, wore sackcloth, and continued weeping. Genesis doesn't rush past his pain. The brothers' wrongdoing affected more than Joseph: their deception left their father mourning without knowing that his son was still alive.

discoveries.title: A New Household in Egypt
discoveries.narration: Now we leave Jacob's camp and follow Joseph into Egypt. The merchants sell him to an official who serves Pharaoh and is chief of the guard. Joseph has arrived in a new land as a slave. His story is far from over, but this chapter closes at the doorway of a very different household.

interaction.prompt: Which Egyptian official bought Joseph from the merchants?

progressiveHints.text: He served Pharaoh, but he wasn't Pharaoh himself.
The verse gives him a particular responsibility: chief of the guard.
Joseph will live in this official's household. Don't confuse him with the king of Egypt.

discoveries.explanation: Potiphar was a court official of Pharaoh and chief of the guard. Genesis 37 ends with Joseph sold into his service, not raised to power. That's an important place to pause: the dreams haven't been fulfilled, and Joseph's situation has changed completely. We'll follow his life in this household in the next episode.
